name: Prodigy Math
line: Prodigy puts math questions inside a fantasy game. In AMP, the problem is the unit, and every answer sets the next.
description: AMP vs Prodigy Math: Prodigy sets math questions inside a fantasy game. In AMP, the problem is the unit, with teaching and assessment at every one.
verdict: Prodigy Math sets its questions inside a fantasy game, where a right answer casts a spell in a battle [7]. It sets question difficulty from a grade level [8]. In AMP, the problem is the unit. Every answer updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Prodigy the unit is a battle in a fantasy game: a right answer to a math question casts a spell, and wins earn coins, gear and pets [7]. In a study Prodigy ran, fourth graders averaged 5.42 hours answering questions in a school year [8]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [14].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After every answer AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. In Prodigy a student who misses a question gets a second try [8], and the question screen offers video lessons and hint bubbles [2]. We found no worked steps after an answer in the pages we read [1][2]. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect [13].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers and keeps a separate level for each part of math, so a learner further along in one part than another gets work at both levels. Prodigy runs a placement test the first time a student plays [2]. After that, question difficulty follows a grade: the one the student or teacher picks, the placement test's, and a grade its algorithm assesses from recent answers [8]. Its study reports the algorithm's grade as one number per student [8].

rows.start: A placement test the first time a student plays sets a starting grade [2]. Teachers can also get a progress snapshot twice a year [1].
rows.teaching: Video lessons and hint bubbles on the question screen [2]. A student who misses gets a second try [8].
rows.next: Difficulty follows a grade: chosen, from the placement test, or assessed from recent answers. The algorithm brings in prerequisite or harder skills [8]. Teachers can assign skills [2].
rows.mastery: No published mastery rule found in the pages we read [1][4].
rows.review: No scheduled review of earlier skills found in the pages we read [1][2].
rows.print: Some accounts can print curated worksheets based on the learner's Practice Areas report [5]. No answer keys found in the pages we read [5].
rows.adult: Little to prepare [6]. Teachers can set assignments, tests, goals and in-game rewards [2]. Parents can set goals and send rewards [4].
rows.reports: Teacher reports by strand and skill [2]. Monthly report cards for parents [4].
rows.evidence: Studies run or paid for by Prodigy, none randomized [6][7][8][9]. Evidence for ESSA lists no qualifying study [11].

theirs: Prodigy Math is a fantasy game for grades 1 to 8 from Prodigy Education [1]. Prodigy calls it a supplemental tool, used beside classroom teaching [3][8].

A student walks a wizard avatar through the game world. Meeting a monster starts a battle, and casting a spell takes a right answer to a math question. Wins earn coins, gear and pets [7]. A placement test runs the first time a student plays. After that an algorithm adjusts difficulty from recent answers and brings in prerequisite or harder skills [2][8]. The question screen offers video lessons and hint bubbles, and teachers can assign skills and set class goals and rewards [2].
credit: In the Johns Hopkins evaluation, students nearly unanimously said it made math easier and more fun [6].
Its algorithm adjusts difficulty from a student's recent answers and brings in prerequisite skills [8].

theirs: Prodigy's page for administrators says it has been independently evaluated and meets ESSA Tier 3 [3]. The Tier 3 sign-off we found sits in a study written by Prodigy staff: 448 fourth graders in one southern U.S. district in 2018-19, with no comparison group [8]. Students averaged 5.42 hours and 662 questions for the year. Accuracy in the game correlated with state test scores (r = .44), and the number of questions answered much less (r = .12). Two Johns Hopkins researchers wrote that they believe the study meets Tier 3, and its authors say causal claims cannot be made [8].

Johns Hopkins' Center for Research and Reform in Education evaluated Prodigy in seven schools of one district, 577 students in kindergarten through grade 5, with funding from Prodigy [6][7]. The design was correlational. For fourth graders, each extra question answered was linked to 0.00113 more points on the Texas state test, roughly 888 questions for one point. Questions answered at home showed no significant link, and students who used it most did not do significantly better than middle users [6][7].

Prodigy's research page cites up to 5x greater improvement with heavy use [10]. That figure comes from a company study in California that compared school grades by how much they used Prodigy. Its authors call the effects small, found no significant difference within cohorts, and write that the findings do not qualify for ESSA Tier II [9]. Prodigy's 2025 state reports, such as one on Texas grade 3, compare high-usage schools with the state average, with no matched comparison group [12]. Every study we found was run or paid for by Prodigy, and none is randomized. Evidence for ESSA lists Prodigy as "No studies met inclusion requirements" [11].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect (0.49), against 0.32 for giving the correct answer and 0.05 for marking right or wrong only [13]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve mathematics performance [14]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Prodigy Math?
questions.answer: Prodigy sets math questions inside a fantasy game, where a right answer casts a spell [7], and sets question difficulty from a grade level [8]. In AMP the problem is the unit: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Prodigy Math work?
questions.answer: Every study we found was run or paid for by Prodigy, and none is randomized [6][7][8][9]. The Johns Hopkins evaluation linked roughly 888 questions to one point on the Texas state test [6]. Evidence for ESSA lists no study of Prodigy that met its requirements [11].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
